utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First of all, does everybody hear me? I would like to be sure that everybody understands me and hears me. Turning to the Defence, are you hearing me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Turning to the Registrar, would you please give us the case numbers of the cases that are on the roll for today?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case IT-95-14-T, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking about the accused, can we ask for the General Blaskic to be brought in now, brought into the courtroom? General Blaskic, do you hear me in your own language? THE ACCUSED [In translation] Mr. President, I can hear you very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First of all, turning to the Office of the Prosecutor, could you please tell us who is representing the Prosecution today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, your Honours. My name is Mark Harmon and appearing with me is Mr. Gregory Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, Russell Hayman and Anto Nobilo appearing on behalf of the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This hearing has two parts, (1) General Blaskic has again filed a brief with the Trial Chamber, he is asking for provisional release; (2) ever since 26th November the Trial Chamber has been reviewing an application from the accused in order to compel the Prosecutor to produce discovery materials. In the order, about which I will ask for your opinion, we are going to make a suggestion, but we will deal with these one after the other in this hearing, both aspects of the problems that are facing us today. Seeing that everybody is here representing the Defence, I would like to ask the Defence whether it is ready, Mr. Hayman, Mr. Nobilo, whether you are prepared to argue for the request for provisional release of your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would first like to argue the motion for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is the Office of the Prosecutor prepared to respond to the first arguments on the problem of the provisional release of General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we are.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then I would now turn to my colleagues. From what we have just said, we will first of all take up the question for provisional release which was filed before this Chamber, I can recall this, in an application which is dated 11th December 1996. Mr. Hayman, Mr. Nobilo, would you please present the arguments for this application? Mr. Nobilo, I am giving the floor to you now. Please turn your microphone on. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you have received a written motion pursuant to Rule 65 for provisional release until the beginning of trial for General Tihomir Blaskic. We all know that in order for someone to be provisionally released there has to be exceptional circumstances. The host country has to be heard and the Trial Chamber has to be satisfied that the accused will appear for trial upon all summons and that he will not pose any danger to any victim, witness or other person. Therefore, the first point that we are going to argue, and this Chamber will have to establish, is the existence or lack of exceptional circumstances in this particular case. Your Honours, we are all aware, and you most of all, of the difficulties this Tribunal is faced with. The International Tribunal finds itself in a very special situation. You do not have a police of your own and you do not belong to any State which controls any particular territory. You simply do not have the possibility to order and execute by your own authorities the arrest of any detainee. The biggest problem of this trial is how to bring the indictees to justice. Except for General Blaskic, the International Tribunal does not have in its custody any other person of such a high rank or any person of such importance from any of the three parties to the conflict. Unlike national jurisdictions, unlike in national jurisdictions, the indictees here are aware of the possibility to avoid appearing before the Tribunal, because in national jurisdictions if the accused refuses to appear on his own he is apprehended by the police and brought to the court. Here we are aware of this sad circumstance, that many of the indictees enjoy protection of their own countries. They have protection even of the police or military in their own countries. Therefore, the police and soldiers of the United Nations do not dare arrest the indictees in order to avoid shooting and unnecessary casualties, also to avoid a possible resumption of hostilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a special situation of this Tribunal and while viewing the case of General Blaskic, one should bear this particular situation in mind which is different from the situation of any other Tribunal, any other court in the world. So, to sum up the greatest difficulty, the biggest problem, of this Tribunal is the fact that the persons indicted for war crimes could, assisted even by the police or the military, avoid appearing before this Tribunal. No one has appeared voluntarily before this Tribunal and if they do not wish to do so, it is relatively simple for them to avoid it. The political situation in the former Yugoslavia is not a very good one at the moment, and it is not favourable to apprehension of indictees. According to, for example, laws in Serbia, this extraditional surrender is not possible. Croatia has adopted such legislation but with certain objections and reservations, and in Bosnia and Herzegovina after a three-member presidency has been established, it seems that they will no longer be able to execute decisions on surrender. Given that situation, in Croatia even before the legislation, the relevant legislation was passed, General Blaskic had decided to appear voluntarily before this Tribunal. It is obvious that General Blaskic is the only person from all sides, parties to the conflict, who had decided on his own voluntarily to appear before this trial. No one before him did so, and no one, as far as I know, is intending to do so. In this situation, the rank of General Blaskic, who has surrendered himself voluntarily to the Tribunal, it seems to me that this constitutes exceptional circumstances. This is not a rule. This is an exception because we cannot find any similar example. Let me just stress that General Blaskic is a General of the Croatian Defence Council and Croatian army, and this Tribunal does not have in its custody anybody with such a high rank. I believe that these circumstances differentiate General Blaskic from all other indictees and from all other cases being prosecuted before this Tribunal. This, therefore, constitutes an exceptional circumstance which is a positive one, both for the work of this Tribunal and the situation in the former Yugoslavia. I, therefore, believe that all the conditions set forth in Rule 65 have been met. I think that his situation, his very courageous act, should be appropriately valued by this Tribunal, also given in view of the situation in the former Yugoslavia. I think that this should be taken into consideration. We, therefore, believe that all elements, all requirements, for exceptional conditions or special conditions, whatever you want to call them, have been met. If we add to all this the personal situation of General Blaskic, we will see that these circumstances are even more favourable in that respect. General Blaskic was indicted in November '95, and he surrendered himself in good faith to the Tribunal in April '96. He knew that an indictment had been issued, and he knew that the investigation had been completed and he believed that enough evidence had been gathered. So he appeared voluntarily before this Tribunal, rightfully expecting his right to an expeditious trial to be granted. He was also aware of a provision from the criminal code of former Yugoslavia, a provision which is now valid both in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, which says that the accused who is detained in detention, that his trial should begin within two months, two months since the indictment against him was issued. This is a provision which is valid in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the accused should be tried two months after the indictment was issued. This is a similar provision to the provision of this Tribunal which speaks about the right to a fair and expeditious trial. Therefore, he arrived, he presented himself in good faith. He wanted to defend himself and he wanted to clear his name. Six months have passed. The trial has not started yet. A year will probably have passed and the trial would begin and maybe it would not. In its response, the Prosecution stated certain examples, but they keep forgetting that we do not object to the duration of the investigation until the issuance of the indictment, but we do object if from the moment the indictment was issued, the Prosecution states that they are not yet ready because they do not have enough evidence and eight months have passed in the meantime. In that case, we do have objections and we respectfully submit that all these facts point to the conclusion that in the case of General Blaskic exceptional circumstances do exist, and that he is a unique example at this Tribunal, and we do not believe that there are any indications that anybody would be in a similar situation as General Blaskic very soon. Detention is not a sanction. It is not a repression. It is our opinion (and we believe that you will agree with us) detention is just a safety measure to ensure that the indictee will not pose danger for witnesses and victims, that he will not abscond and so on. Therefore, just as any other sanction, it should be minimum, it should be a minimum sanction which is necessary to ensure those objectives. If we analyse the situation of General Blaskic, his behaviour so far and all the facts that have been established so far in this case, then I believe that we can come up with a conclusion that there is no danger that General Blaskic will escape and that he will not appear before this Tribunal if summoned. So General Blaskic again has come to the Hague on his own. He was not under any kind of pressure, and if he arrived here on his own in April, then you can be assured that he would appear before this Tribunal upon any request. The very fact of his coming to the Tribunal on his own is the strongest argument when we say that there is no danger that General Blaskic would either hide or abscond. Not a single fact has been established that General Blaskic would pose any danger for witnesses or victims. If we analyse the file, we can conclude that General Blaskic did not pose any danger for victims or witnesses during the war and especially not now. We have read all the witness statements submitted to us by the Prosecution and we do not have any objection, I do not see any need to influence those witnesses. We are perfectly satisfied with those witnesses and with what they say. Therefore, I believe that circumstances, the situation, of General Blaskic do not point out to any danger of escape or influence of witnesses. But in order to support this and to give full assurances to you, we have proposed a whole range of measures that guarantee that General Blaskic will appear for trial and will not interfere with witnesses. I would like to stress something that may not have been written in our submission, but we propose the provisional release take place until the beginning of the trial and he will be available to you in the conditions set forth by the Trial Chamber. We propose that his ability to travel be limited and that he can reside only in Zagreb. We are, therefore, prepared to hand over his passport and we are prepared to be exposed to any kind of control of your office in Zagreb, by telephone or in any other way. The Republic of Croatia is prepared to give its guarantee, to offer its guarantee, that General Blaskic will return to trial and we propose the bail bond to the amount of 1 million German marks. This is offered to the Tribunal as an additional guarantee that General Blaskic will not go into hiding and that he will come back for trial. Last but not least, General Blaskic is prepared to give his word of honour that he will come back to the Hague, he will come back to the Tribunal for trial and his behaviour so far is a sufficient guarantee in this respect. To sum up, I would like to express my hope that I think it can be concluded that all the conditions, all the requirements, for provisional release have been met. We are proposing that General Blaskic reside in the Republic of Croatia and it is, of course, possible to consult the country in which he will reside and the host country in this case would be, therefore, Republic of Croatia. The Republic of Croatia is prepared to give any assurances, any guarantee, requested by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I turn to Judge Deschenes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo ----

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. We do not hear. The Judge does not have his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: You were talking about some kind of guarantees you would give or insurance policies you would give; I would like to know what kind of a form this possible bail bond would have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, in accordance with your decision, it can be in the form of cash to be submitted to the Tribunal or other irrevocable bank letter of credit to that amount, as you wish, as would be more suitable for you, for technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before we give the floor to the Prosecution, I would like to recall that, according to Rule 65 which speaks about the host country, and I would like to ask the Registrar whether according to this formality which the Trial Chamber, of course, will have to fulfil, I see, apparently, that there is no real definition of the "host country". Could you give us an explanation before I give the floor to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Further to the application of 11th December, from that point on, we wrote to the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs, should the Trial Chamber decide that General Blaskic would be put into provisional release, given provisional release, but would remain here, we received five minutes before this hearing (which I have not yet distributed either to the parties or to the Trial Chamber, but it will be done this morning) a brief response from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs saying to us that it is referring to a letter which is dated 18th July 1996, a letter which deals with the Delalic case. If you will permit me, I will read the letter to you and the letter, of course, will be distributed to you during the morning: "The Dutch government responds as follows: First of all, the Dutch government points out, first, that the Tribunal must decide not to accept a right but under what conditions. The Dutch government has these observations which have a practical nature dealing with provisional release. An accused falls under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal so long as he is incarcerated in the detention unit in Scheveningen. However, if he is released he falls under the jurisdiction of the Netherlands. If he does not have a permit to remain in the Netherlands, the Dutch government, therefore, in that case, pursuant to the law covering foreigners and an application of all of those provisions dealing with the Scheveningen courts, must deport that person to the country from which he comes. "If, however, he were to ask for a request to remain in the country, to the Dutch government, if it is not contrary to the interests of the Netherlands, so long as does not cause any prejudice to the Netherlands, he may be given the right to remain in the country, but this decision falls under the exclusive authority of the Minister of Justice of the Netherlands. "During his stay here, the government of the Netherlands takes no responsibility having to do with any practical questions such as the lodging or the protection or any other surveillance measures which must be taken for him, nor for any conditions which the Tribunal might impose having to do with the release of that person". Signed, legal adviser, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I turn to Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You just mentioned that the government of Croatia is ready to give any guarantees as to the presence of the General before the Tribunal, but you did not explicitly give us a detailed form of these guarantees. What are these guarantees?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the guarantee would be in the form of a statement of the Republic of Croatia in any form that you deem sufficient, whereby the Republic of Croatia as a State would undertake to guarantee that General Blaskic would appear before this Tribunal following your request, and that he would not leave the territory of the city of Zagreb for as long as he awaits the beginning of the trial. Of course, the State is able to ensure that with its police force and using other means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before we give the floor to the Prosecutor, I would like to summarise the response from the Ministry of the Dutch government. If I have understood correctly, General Blaskic, if he were to be released provisionally, would immediately be likely to be deported, unless there be an emergency procedure, according to which he would be given the right to remain in the country which would, of course, be reviewed in accordance with the laws dealing with the status of people who are asking for a temporary asylum right of a government within the European Union. If I have understood it correctly, that is how it has to be interpreted. So, at the current moment, I now turn to Mr. Nobilo and ask, taken into account what has just been read and, of course, having to do with the case law, both of the Dutch government and of the small case law that this Tribunal is beginning to have, because we have already received summary requests for provisional release. Have you undertaken any steps, should your client be released provisionally? Have you made any contacts with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, among others, because I think that would fall under the jurisdiction of that Ministry. I give you the floor now, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have not contacted anyone because, according to our suggestion, General Blaskic would while awaiting trial reside in Zagreb. So we could organise General Blaskic to be transferred to a Croatian aeroplane and to be escorted by the UN police to Croatia, and in this way it would not be necessary to ask any permission from the Dutch government, any kind of residence permit.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is what I did understand, Mr. Nobilo. Your request for provisional release only deals with Zagreb. In other words, your request for provisional release which you have provided does not provide for the possibility -- I see that your associate wants to speak; I will let him speak in a moment -- but if I did understand correctly, your request for provisional release for General Blaskic would take place only in the limited manner of a provisional release in Zagreb. Do we understand ourselves here, one another here? Would you like to add something, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just to confirm, your Honour, I think that is absolutely correct. The proposal is that during any appearances here in The Hague, during the trial of the matter, he would remain in custody in the Netherlands, as has been the case. So we are not proposing any provisional release with release in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This point has been clarified. We do not have to hear from the host country and its representative. We will put into the transcript of this hearing that the Trial Chamber has noted that, despite steps that have been undertaken, the host country apparently did not feel it was necessary to answer this type of invitation to appear here and under these conditions. I will now give the floor to the Prosecution in order to respond to the arguments of the Defence. I would like to recall that, generally speaking, of course, the Judges read any documents which you may exchange with one another. Therefore, perhaps you could underscore the facts which appear to be the most important to you. I now give you the floor, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Your Honour, many of the points that have been raised by Mr. Nobilo were raised previously in his written submission requesting provisional release of General Blaskic. In response to his written submission, we submitted a response. I do not think it would be necessary at this point in time to address each of the points in my written response. I have done so and I think they are expressed very clearly in my written response. However, I would like to just touch upon some points that were raised by Mr. Nobilo in his oral presentation. He did very accurately, I think, sum up for this court the problems that face the Tribunal with a person who has been indicted and who is in the former Yugoslavia. The ability to have that person turned over to the Tribunal is extremely problematic. I would submit to this Court that a guarantee by the Republic of Croatia, given its records in turning over indictees and people who have been in its country, is not comforting and cannot be replied upon. Mr. Nobilo has indicated that General Blaskic is unique in that he is the only person who has been before this Tribunal who has decided to voluntarily appear before it. I would remind this Court that Mr. Drazen Erdemovic, who was recently sentenced by this Court, intended to voluntarily submit himself to this Tribunal but was arrested in the former Yugoslavia and eventually brought to this Tribunal by process, legal process, of the Tribunal. But he also had an intention to surrender this to this Court and I think the Court, in terms of its sentencing of Mr. Erdemovic, recognised that voluntary intention and took that into consideration. I would submit to this Court that intention to voluntarily surrender was true in Mr. Erdemovic's case and Mr. Erdemovic did not receive any special consideration, in terms of his custodial status. Mr. Erdemovic remained in custody at the Tribunal's detention facility with the Rules and regulations applied fully to him. General Blaskic has appeared voluntarily before this Tribunal, and that voluntary surrender has been recognised by this Tribunal. He is in a custodial situation, a detention situation, that is far more privileged than any other detainee held in the Tribunal's custody. So I think it is accurate to say that this Court has taken into consideration, and President Cassese has taken into consideration the voluntary nature of General Blaskic's surrender. The other issues that have been raised I have mentioned to this Trial Chamber have been addressed by me in my written submission to the Court. I am prepared to rely upon my written submission. I have nothing further to say, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I give the floor to Judge Deschenes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Harmon, what importance would you attach to the security that is offered by the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I explained in my written response ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Yes, but I ----

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: --- but I did not attach much to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Yes, that is my question mark. I have read your response, but I am a little puzzled by the fact that you just offhand say, "Well, you cannot rely on that, it has no value", after all, there would be a monetary guarantee of one million deutschemarks that the accused would show up, which means that should he fail, then obviously that guarantee would be forfeited.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is one factor, certainly a monetary guarantee, that is available to this Court, but I think the Court has to consider the full ramifications of a failure to reappear on this case by General Blaskic. The guarantee, certainly money is forfeitable,. It happens frequently in situations where accused have put up bail and they do not appear. What the judicial authorities are left with, frankly, is money and in national states they have the ability, because they have police forces, to go secure the arrest of the person who has jumped his bail. We do not have that opportunity with this Tribunal. Again, if he does not appear and he forfeits the bail, this Trial Chamber will once again have to rely upon the judicial authorities and the authorities of the Republic of Croatia to return him. At the base, your Honour, that is a very fragile and feeble guarantee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: I would be normally prepared to follow your reasoning at the national level where bails usually are for amounts which are manageable, but in this case it seems that the bail that is offered is substantial. I am just wondering whether one can say easily, "Well, he may easily jump his bail and not show up". Somebody will be held then holding the bag. What would happen to the million deutschemarks? Do you think that the guarantor would easily appreciate and contribute to that situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two responses to that: (1) it depends on whose money it is. If it is the State's money, this is a State, the Republic of Croatia, that has not turned over people, in the face of the appropriate legislation, the fact that there have been indictees on its territory who it is aware have been on its territory and it has not turned them over. If it is the State's money and the State forfeits the money, we are again stuck with the guarantee of the State to retrieve the person who was supposed to be before this Tribunal. My own view, your Honour, is that this Trial Chamber in its previous decision believed that bail was insufficient to guarantee the presence of the accused. I share that judgment. So, I do not think in this particular case that justice can a have a price, that one can buy his way out of custody. I would urge this Court to look beyond the potential of forfeited bail, to look to who the guarantor is. The guarantor in this case, if General Blaskic goes back to Croatia, is the Republic of Croatia. That is the entity that must return him. As I have submitted to your Honours, that is not a comforting record that is before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You are welcome, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. I would like to turn to the Defence and ask two questions. The first one which is perhaps indiscreet you may not want to answer. Is it Croatia or General Blaskic who is responsible for the guarantee or for the bail, having to do with the other accused in this case, but we do say it is true that General Blaskic appeared apparently spontaneously, but it is true as well that, apparently, in Croatia there are four or five other accused who appear in the same case file, and up to this point, as far as I know, Croatia has not fulfilled its obligations having to do with the other accused, which of course leaves us somewhat confused as to the guarantees that Croatia might give, having to do with the return of the accused to this Tribunal. On these two points, Mr. Nobilo, could you give us some clarifications?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, as to the bail bond, I will speak to you quite openly. This is the money of General Blaskic, his family and his relatives. They do not have that kind of cash, but they will mortgage all the real estate they have, all the houses that are their property and they will get a loan from the bank and submit that money. They do not have that amount in cash, but they do have property, real estate, and they can obtain a loan from the bank. So we are talking about the money owned by the family and relatives of General Blaskic. It is not the money of the State. As for the Republic of Croatia, my opinion differs in this respect. I see the Republic of Croatia as the only country that has passed a law on co-operation with the Tribunal. Furthermore, no citizens of the Republic of Croatia with permanent residence in Croatia has been indicted by this Tribunal. The indictees are Croats with permanent residence in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I do not have any information at my disposal that any of the indictees are currently residing in the Republic of Croatia. I only have the statement issued by Mr. Mate Granic, the Foreign Minister of Croatia. He stated that none of the indictees is currently in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, except for Mr. Aleksovski, in whose case the legal procedure has been concluded. From what I have heard from the reports in the Republic, I do not have any official information about that, his extradition is underway. There are certain health issues, health concerns. So the Republic of Croatia has arrested the only indictee at its disposal and conducted the legal procedure and he will be extradited, and even Mr. Aleksovski is not a resident of the Republic of Croatia, a citizen of the Republic of Croatia. So, if we viewed this situation in realistic terms in the territory of former Yugoslavia, we have to conclude that the Republic of Croatia is ready to co-operate with the International Tribunal to the greatest extent. The office of the Tribunal was opened in Zagreb, in Croatia, a long time ago when it was not possible to do so in other countries. This Tribunal does not seek the extradition of any Croatian citizen with permanent residence in Croatia. So I feel that the guarantees issued by the Republic of Croatia which has shown itself to be willing to implement both the Dayton Agreements and all the other international agreements it has undertaken to implement, that it is the most willing of all the countries, sides, to the conflict. I feel that this guarantee would have much more power than the Prosecution is willing to accord it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, in the light of what the Defence said about the readiness of the government of Croatia to co-operate with passing the law, what is your assessment of the practical aspect of this co-operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is one thing, your Honour, to set up and permit the International Tribunal to have an office in Zagreb; it is an entirely different thing to not arrest people who have been indicted and who are in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. I do not want to make too fine a distinction, as Mr. Nobilo has said, but his distinction is that there are no permanent residents in Croatia who have been arrested. It is true, some of the indictees are Croats from Bosnia, but residency is not the test; the test is that a national State that receives a warrant of arrest from this Tribunal has an obligation to execute that warrant, whether or not a person is a resident of the country. In that respect, there have been indictees who are not residents, who have been on the territory of Croatia, and who have not been arrested by the Croatian authorities. So, my sense very clearly is, yes, Croatia has co-operated in some respects, in that regard they deserve credit, we have an office in Croatia, but the real test of co-operation is a willingness to arrest and turn over to this Tribunal people who have been indicted. In that respect, the Republic of Croatia has failed, quite simply. I cite in my response comments by President Cassese that the Republic of Croatia was, undoubtedly, in breach of international legal obligations upon it. That has been a finding by the President of this Tribunal. I cite too the Aleksovski case. That is a situation where Mr. Aleksovski, apparently, was arrested in May 1996. He still has not been turned over to this Tribunal. So, we have to be very clear in what we are talking about in this hearing. This hearing is not whether Croatia has co-operated in allowing the Tribunal to set up an office; this hearing is about whether the guarantee of the Republic of Croatia is something that can be relied upon when it says, "We will guarantee that General Blaskic when he comes to our territory will be returned to this Tribunal." In that respect, your Honour, I would say the record is not comforting whatsoever. I have nothing further to say on that point, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like to put this question back into its context. I think it is only because the Defence raised the argument, among others, in support of its request that it would bring in the guarantee of the Republic of Croatia. The Tribunal, of course, is very curious to know what type of guarantee Croatia could bring. Of course, we are not talking about keeping the accused because it is not giving us other accused. We are dealing here with the request for provisional release by General Blaskic, because the Defence thought that it should bring any additional argument, among others, that is the argument of the guarantee from the Republic of Croatia. We would have to know exactly what that meant. Before we finish with this part of our discussion, I would like to turn to General Blaskic and ask him what comments he would like to make, if he does have any comments he would like to make. General Blaskic, would you please stand and tell us if you have any comments to make on all of the discussion that you have heard up to this point, both the comments from the Prosecution and from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have nothing further to add, except to say what my Defence counsel stated, that I am prepared to answer the summons of this Tribunal at any time and to report here, because my goal was to face trial at the Tribunal. I think that myself and my family are the most willing to have this trial start. This is what I said to Mr. Marro, that I have my honour and I want the trial to start as soon as possible because this is the only solution that I can see in this situation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have now finished our discussion having to do with the request for provisional release. I would like to turn to my colleagues. (The learned Judges conferred) The Tribunal will now suspend the hearing until 11 o'clock. The response of the Tribunal to the request for provisional release will be given tomorrow morning at 11 o'clock. The hearing is adjourned and we will resume at 11.00. 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The hearing is now resumed. This hearing will now consider the issue of an application which was filed on 26th November 1996 by the accused and by his counsel, with the purposes of compelling the production of discovery materials by the Prosecution. The Prosecutor has responded to this and this response was on 11th December. The Defence itself answered the arguments of the Prosecution on 16th December. The Trial Chamber, of course, reviewed the documents and will hear the parties with it being understood that before that perhaps, giving the floor to the Defence, the Judges would be inclined to ask both parties before the issues are treated at what point today we can reach an agreement. I recall that in his application the Defence counsel presented with a certain number of arguments a request for discovery, first, of the statement of the accused; second, the statement of the witnesses; third, the list of the Prosecution witnesses and, generally speaking, all evidence submitted in support of the indictment pursuant to Rule 47 and, fifth, I am now speaking about the most important points of course, a very important point also, the exculpatory evidence which may be produced and is requested from the Defence to the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 68. I would like to make summary as objectively as possible, all of this is aimed at having almost complete production of discovery materials, all materials that the Prosecution may have. The Prosecutor answered this. I am now going through the legal orders, having to do with the interpretations of Rules 66, 67 and 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I will go back to what I was saying before. The Prosecution responded to this application, considering that it was not its responsibility to give a positive answer, that itself it had already pursuant to the orders that have been given by the Trial Chamber, having to do with the witnesses that have been called who were either agreed or not agreed to appear before the Trial Chamber, and the Prosecutor considers that having to do with the exculpatory evidence, that it had already responded, according to 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and that it also rejected a certain number of assertions which had been made specifically having to do with the evidence that had been given by Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Prosecution. The Defence has just answered, as I have said. This was a rather recent response. I received the French translation yesterday afternoon. The response was on 16th December, with a more legal argument having to do with the incorrect, in its opinion, interpretation by the Prosecution of the texts which are in effect, that is 66, 67 and 68, and considers that the Prosecution was limiting too restrictively the interpretation of the terms of the word "statement". If I can summarise some of the difficulties of the production of discovery materials on both sides? First of all, this is an important problem for which there is a real dispute between the Prosecution and the Defence. Both will have the opportunity to express themselves on this point. But the Judges of this Trial Chamber are concerned, as we have already said several weeks ago, by the speed which is appropriate for these hearings, so that the trial takes place as quickly as possible. Of course, the Judges can only observe that so long as there are significant disputes having to do with the production of evidence is concerned, the trial will be blocked. Therefore, the desire of the Judges to go forward quickly and the question which must be previously asked and I, first of all, give the floor to the Defence since it made its presentation, I would ask now Mr. Hayman because, Mr. Hayman -- you or Mr. Nobilo -- you did show a positive -- whether you a show a positive or negative chart of those materials that were given to you, I am not asking this so that you can answer that everything was negative, but I want to know whether now, since the last time we spoke, having to do with the list of the Prosecution witnesses, are there any positive factors in this communication or the discovery that was given to you by the Prosecutor, and today where are we when it has to do with the subject of your application having to do specifically with discovery? Have I been clear? Do you understand what I have been to ask you? In other words, I am not going to give you the floor immediately to argue. I would simply, first of all, like to try to make a distinction between the possible lines of agreement there could be and if there is no agreement at all the Trial Chamber will decide, not tomorrow of course, but will try to reach a decision as quickly as possible. I now give you the floor about the previous question Mr. Hayman. I am not asking you to argue but, first, to talk about the chart that we have talked about, and I will ask the Prosecution whether the Prosecution feels that it has really acquitted itself of all its obligations. Then you will speak and then I will give the floor to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. If I understand the Court properly, what I would address now is simply that all of the items we have sought in our motion and in our reply brief are still before the Court, save one, and that is so-called item E in our original motion which was on page 10 of the English, a motion we filed, "Evidence submitted to the Tribunal in support of the indictment pursuant to Rule 47". We have gotten significant additional materials in that category since the filing of our motion. I do not think there are any issues there that should be before the Court; rather, we are still reviewing the materials that have been produced and working with the Prosecution to try to resolve any remaining questions on that category.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Therefore, this is the first point of agreement. I turn to the Prosecution, it would appear that the Defence considers -- I repeat now -- when it comes to its application of 26th November, point E, which says "Evidence submitted to the Tribunal in support of the indictment pursuant to Rule 47", the Defence considers that for the time being, and conditional on any in-depth review it will make, the obligation for discovery was fulfilled. I believe that is the opinion of the Defence. I will turn to the Prosecution, do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, certainly in respect of item E, we are complying, we intend to fully comply in the future and we have communications regularly in regard to items that may have been inadvertently not sent, and there is an instant and immediate compliance in that respect. I would also suggest, your Honour, that in respect of item K, that is Rule 61 materials, since there was no Rule 61 hearing, that issue is no longer viable. The rest, your Honour ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What page are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 25 of the defendant's motion to compel discovery.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You agree, Mr. Hayman, that this was a mistake? You do understand that there was no Rule 61 hearing in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We were referring to the Rajic matter, your Honour, that is correct. So K can be consolidated, if you will, with the other request for other Rule 61 materials.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution, would you like to add anything else before I give the floor back to Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, we are now going to start with your original request. Could you synthesize the points on which there is disagreement? I am not asking you to argue and specifically not to argue from a legal point of view but, rather, on the interpretation that you have of 66, 67 and 68. What I would like is for you to tell us now what, in your opinion, should still be supplied to you, having to do with your request, we are still remaining within your original request, in order to make the discussions clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Starting with the first category, statements of the accused. I think there is disagreement as to the definition of "statement" within the meaning of Rule 66(A), both in terms of whether a statement has to have been taken directly by the Office of the Prosecutor or not. We contend that a statement can be taken by any party. It is still a statement. It is not a statement only if it is taken by the Office of the Prosecutor. The dispute there involves the phraseology of the Rule. The Prosecution reads it in one way and we read it in a broader way. Again, if I am not to argue the matter at this point, I will simply state what I think the areas of disagreement are. The second area of disagreement with respect to statements of the accused again goes to the meaning of the term "statement", and derives from the assertion in the Prosecution's opposition brief at page 6 that, "A statement is a formal declaration given under oath or at least signed or acknowledged". We do not agree that that interpretation of the word "statement" should be read into Rule 66(A). We think a statement can be other things -- the notes of a witness, a written memorialization in the form of memoranda of someone interviewing a witness. We think those types of documents can be statements. Thus, we are concerned that because the Prosecution and the Defence have a different view of this very, very important phrase, that there are materials not being produced under Rule 66(A) that should be produced. That second element and, in fact, both elements ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I interrupted you. We have chosen a certain method to use in order to move forward. I would now like to turn to the Prosecution and summarise. For Mr. Hayman, the dispute has to do with the interpretation of 66(A) which I can recall makes disclosure by the Prosecution necessary. Do we agree what the dispute is, that is, the notion of what the statements are? For you, Prosecution, and we will give you the -- the gathering of statements is more restrictive than the interpretation given to this concept by the Defence. I now give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we agree that that is an area of dispute in respect of statements. The definition of what constitutes a statement and the breadth and the intention of the Rule itself.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is a point on which you will argue. I give the floor to you again, Mr. Hayman, and we will now move to the question of the statements by witnesses. Where is the dispute on this point, from a factual point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The dispute, your Honour, with respect to witnesses encompasses the same two issues under Rule 66(A) as we just discussed concerning statements from the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose at least you agree on what the disagreement is?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We agree on the disagreement, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is how things always begin and then one moves forwards, that people first have to agree on what they disagree on. Mr. Hayman, you still have the floor. The Prosecution witnesses, which is D in your application, has to do with a list of Prosecution witnesses. Do we consider that this problem was solved through the very long dispute having to do with the protection of the witnesses? Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We maintain it was not, your Honour, because although we have been given now the identities of a number of witnesses and the statements of, in fact, I think over 100 witnesses, we have not been given a list. What the requirement, we believe, of Rule 67(A) is, is that when the Prosecution forms an intent, a present intent, to call certain witnesses and not to call others, it has an obligation to notify us of those names. That raises a couple of possibilities; one is that of the witness statements that they disclosed to us that were included in the supporting material to the indictment in November 1995, there may be individuals whom they no longer intend to call. Those persons would not be on their list and it is important that we have that information. Also, there may be other individuals who they intend to call as witnesses from whom they have no statements. We will only learn of those individuals if we, in fact, get the list called for under 67(A). So that is why we still believe we should receive in a timely fashion, on a date certain, a list of intended Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, the dispute here, therefore, appears not have to do with a legal issue, but on a factual issue. I turn to the Prosecution, what is your feeling about point D of the Prosecution witnesses? These are the witnesses which are supposed to accompany the initial indictment and then, of course, the modified indictment as it was modified about one months ago. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the dispute on Rule 67 does not centre on the interpretation of it so much as to the timing of when the production should be required. So, I think that is the heart of the dispute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I summarise: you argued about the interpretation of subRule 66(A) specifically, and now having to do with the timing of when the list should be produced and you also say as well as the expert witnesses. We do agree on that, do we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Under Rule 67(A), your Honour, yes; the key phrase being as early as reasonably practicable and in any event prior to the commencement of the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Therefore, we have now solved for the moment subRule (E). Now we move to the third source of problems which seem to be the exculpatory evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. With respect to that, what we have is a legal position taken by the Prosecution that the Defence has not made a prima facie showing that it possesses, that it the Prosecution possesses, the categories, any of the categories, of information that we described in our original motion. The Court will recall we set forth at pages 13 through 21 approximately eight pages of description of information which we believe the Prosecution possesses in, perhaps, various forms. We asked for its production under Rule 68. They have answered that we have not made a prima facie showing that they possess it and that they need not make any other response. Our response to that, your Honour, is that under Rule 68 the burden is on them to produce exculpatory information. We are trying to assist in that process by specifying what we think would be exculpatory, and that because they possess the information only they know specifically in what form, in what document, on what tape they possess it and they have an obligation to respond substantively, i.e. do they have it, do they not? If they have it, do they disagree as to whether it is exculpatory or not?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. I will turn to Mr. Harmon. Is this exactly what the dispute is about and only about this? I thought that the dispute was a more legal issue. One feels that Mr. Hayman is saying that the dispute has to do with whether there is an existence or not an existence of these elements and, of course, in this form, implicitly, it is implied that if you agreed on the existence in your case file of all of these elements, that at least you would agree with Mr. Hayman on the point that all of these elements could give exculpatory information, or are you saying that this is not the responsibility of the Office of the Prosecutor? What is your feeling about this? I am trying to limit exactly what the points of the dispute are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in response to that, let me start by saying what the dispute is not about. The Defence has contended that in its reply to our response that we contend, the Prosecutor contends, that it has no obligation to search for exculpatory material under Rule 68. We reject that characterisation. We do an obligation to search for exculpatory material. We have been abiding by that obligation. The Defence has been receiving what is, arguably, exculpatory information. The dispute that I see in this case is, essentially, whether we have been complying with our obligations under Rule 68 and whether we intend to continue to do so. The Defence in this case has said that it -- on page 5 of its motion -- knows we have certain evidence that we are, essentially, not giving to the Defence. So they have set forth their position that they know we have this evidence and, it seems to me, without arguing, there has to be a showing, at least some degree of showing, that the Prosecution has the evidence sought.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just a moment please, Mr. Harmon. So there is a dispute about whether or not this evidence exists?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is a dispute, your Honour, as to whether it exists in the possession, custody and control of the Prosecutor. Secondly, there is a dispute as to whether the evidence identified by Mr. Hayman in his request to compel discovery is, in fact, exculpatory. There is a third dispute and that is whether or not the exculpatory evidence rule can be used to subvert the reciprocal discovery provisions of the Rules themselves. So those are the areas of our dispute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There is a dispute having to do whether or not these elements exist, elements that the Defence has mentioned, for example, that might throw some light on the discussions having to do with any kind of directives or any declarations which show the efforts of the HVO to encourage the various measures, having to do with the protection of civilian population. Everybody understands this very easily; that the Defence is saying that you have these elements. This is the first point of the dispute, if we use this, and the Prosecution says that it has to prove that it has this material. So, legally speaking, we have to find out whether or not it is the Prosecution or -- well, the Defence has to prove that it exists, or whether the Prosecution has to say, "I have it" or "I do not have it". Then we have to know whose responsibility it is to show that these elements exist. Lastly, the Prosecution is saying that, in any event, this type of request from the Defence could not contribute to relieving it of reciprocal discovery. So should I understand, Mr. Harmon, on this last point that if, for example, firstly, you say that you did have all of these elements and then, secondly, you considered that one could find exculpatory material in them, if you had all of this, what is your position having to do with the obligation of reciprocal discovery?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Our view, your Honour, is this is a request for reciprocal discovery and compliance with, essentially, what is a request to look at all the Prosecutor's file would obligate the Defence to permit us to examine the relevant documents that they intend to introduce as evidence in the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are not quite answering what I was asking. What I mean is if the Defence were to say, there is agreement, "We will give you our entire case file", what would your point of view be on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We would obviously comply with the Rules and the obligations set forth in those Rules. There would be no question about that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All right. I am not responsible for defending the interests of either of the parties. We will now go on. There is a dispute which has to do with three points. This is now the third issue, the third issue that we are going to review. We have gotten to E or F, I believe it was F. Mr. Hayman, you go even further than that, if I have understood this correctly, because you say in your brief that the lack of proof can also be exculpatory. This is very subtle or an elementary thing. This is a very subtle point. Could you explain what you mean by this to the Trial Chamber because when we try to follow you, we can go as far as character, as they say, if there is no indictment, we could say that that would be a complete exculpatory situation. Could you explain exactly what you mean by your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For example, if in a case alleging rape, if there were laboratory tests performed that were inconclusive, that did not show the presence of a substance in or on the victim that connected the accused to the crime, that would be a lack of evidence, a lack of affirmative scientific evidence, linking the suspect to the crime in that way. In that situation, if the Prosecution possessed that laboratory finding (and there is a case in the United States on this very subject), it cannot conceal that from the Defence on the grounds that is a lack of evidence, that is not affirmative evidence and so it does not implicate the obligation to produce exculpatory evidence; rather, the Prosecution would have an obligation to produce that laboratory test finding because it shows a lack of scientific evidence connecting the accused to the crime. By analogy, we have argued here that in four specific areas (and we have specified four specific areas) where we believe there is a lack of Prosecution evidence, and we would seek at trial to introduce an agreement between the parties that the Prosecution does lack evidence in these four areas. Now the Prosecution has responded, "Well, you can argue that at trial, but that is something for the evidence to show at trial". The problem is, and why I do not think that is satisfactory, take, for example, item 3, the lack of any electronic intercepts showing that the accused had any real time commanding control through modern telecommunications over any of the relevant forces. Perhaps if the Prosecution put on the witness stand at trial all the relevant persons who might know of the existence of such evidence, and we could ask those individuals, "Do you know of any such evidence?" And they all answered "No", we might be able to show in the record of the trial that there was an absence or a lack of any evidence showing real time modern telecommunications Commander control systems within the HVO in central Bosnia during the relevant time period. But if they do not put those people on the stand, we will never be able to show an affirmative lack of evidence. We can argue the Prosecution did not put any in, but we cannot argue that there is no evidence known to either party. That is what we would like to be able to do in these four areas. I agree this is a subtle issue, not the most important in our motion, but still one we feel is important, and I think that is the essence of the disagreement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanations. Mr. Harmon, what do you think about this? The Defence is not giving up on this point. What is your opinion about this? Then I will turn to my colleagues to see whether or not we could not solve this problem as quickly as possible. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have a substantial dispute with the Defence on this point. The exculpatory evidence Rule imposes upon the Prosecutor an obligation to go through its files and find positive elements that could be arguably exculpatory. This request, if I understand it, is an effort to seek a stipulation from the Prosecutor which I mentioned in my response that the Prosecutor has no intention of giving. It also is an opportunity or an attempt to virtually browse through everything the Prosecutor has, because the absence of evidence is licensed to inspect large portions of documents and large portions of evidence in the possession and control of the Prosecutor, because there are some pieces of evidence that simply do not address what is requested in items 1, 2, 3 and 4 and which would, therefore, have to be revealed by this essentially request for negative information. That is our position on this, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like to turn to my colleagues. (The learned Judges conferred) Mr. Hayman, you have, in fact, said that this is somewhat of a fragile argument. In your brief you ask that this could be brought up in trial. We do, we have reached the very limits of the trial and the Trial Chamber says that it does not have to make a pronouncement about this and that during the trial you would take advantage of this if it is advantageous to you. So we will not discuss it any further and move to point H, evidence gathered and provided to the Prosecution by Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There, your Honours, we believe that there is likely significant evidence that will affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence and Prosecution witnesses by virtue of the fact that there have been two investigative efforts in this case. The first investigative effort was by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina against the accused. Charges were brought in a Court in Sarajevo, if not elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina, against the accused as a result of that investigative effort. Those charges are different, considerably different, in materials respects to the charges in either of the original indictment or the amended indictment here. I think, we certainly believe, that where you have had two different investigative efforts into the same matter, necessarily there will be inconsistencies, there will be differences of viewpoint. There will be multiple witness statements containing different statements. We all know that, I would submit, from our work in the criminal justice system. This request at its fundamental basis is an attempt to ask the Prosecution to please review material they have received from the government and from agents of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, secondly, if they know of such material, they also have an obligation, we think, to carefully scrutinise that material for any inconsistencies or other gaps, holes, differences or contradictions that may bear on the credibility of the evidence they will be presenting. My suggestion was that they simply give us this material so that all of those differences and inconsistencies and contradictions could come to light. They have stated they are not willing to do that. So be it. I still think they have a particularised obligation to review that material and make a production. I think, perhaps, for purposes of this hearing we should categorise this as a subcategory of exculpatory evidence that we are continuing to request.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This the way I had understood it. This is part of the evidence which you considered could be used as exculpatory material for your client. Could you give us your opinion about this, Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sense a difference between the request that was made in the original request to compel discovery under H, that was access to all the materials that were provided by the Bosnian government to us, to now a request for us to review evidence that has been supplied by the Bosnian government to see if it may fall within the purview of Rule 68. We fully intend to review all of the evidence that we have in respect of General Blaskic and will comply with our Rule 68 obligations. That is the way I understand the current request. The request, if it has not been changed and if the Defence continues to request all evidence that has been supplied to us by Bosnia and Herzegovina, we would object to that because it is far too broad. Our position is that the appropriate place to raise issues of the untrustworthiness of the evidence is at trial, and it should not be license for the Defence to rummage through vast amounts of material that are in the possession of the Tribunal in the Prosecutor's Office. So our position, your Honour, is if the Defence request is for us to review the evidence we have received from Bosnia and Herzegovina with an eye to potentially exculpatory evidence, we will do so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we accept that this request which the accused continues to make has to do with evidence which was supplied by Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Prosecution. I understood at this point there is no dispute, that there is evidence which was given to the Prosecution by the Bosnia and Herzegovina authorities. The dispute specifically has to do with the timing, is it at the trial or is it now? I also point out that the Prosecution is prepared, as is the case with the other elements, to look through all its materials supplied by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina which might prove to be exculpatory. Now we will take up point I which has to do with evidence in the Prosecution's possession, including evidence submitted at the Tribunal in connection with the indictment of Rajic, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. There we believe that this body of material is of itself exculpatory. There are acts allegedly committed by this other individual for which he has been charged, for which our client has not been charged, even though this other individual was within a chain of command of the HVO in central Bosnia. That raises some very basic questions about if misconduct, if crimes occurred by subordinates of the accused for which the accused has not been charged, the question is, why? Was there a lack of command of control? Was there a lack of discipline? Was there a lack of responsiveness to orders of the accused? We do not know. We have been given nothing to indicate why, apparently, the Prosecution views no command responsibility on the part of the accused for these acts. We are concerned that there is exculpatory material of that nature in this material and that we have not received it. (The learned Judges conferred)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could you explain briefly this, Prosecution, so we can know whether this is still going to be an area of dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I stated in my written response, certainly we will review the evidence in the Rajic case for exculpatory material. If we find potentially exculpatory material, we are prepared to present it to the Defence. However, the request, and we resist the request, to have the Defence obtain all those highly confidential materials, examine those highly confidential materials and, essentially, be permitted to go fishing through clearly large amounts of material that have nothing to do with this particular defendant -- so, our view is, as I said, we are prepared to review the materials for potentially exculpatory materials and we will provide the Defence with that information. If the Defence has a dispute as to how the Prosecutor should charge its cases, then I think the appropriate time and place for that issue to be raised is at trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber tends to agree with that reasoning, because each time a problem will arise before this Tribunal having to do with command responsibility at a high level, as I have said this morning, this is perhaps the first time -- I do not know all the cases of this Tribunal but I believe this is the first time -- that the accused has such a high rank and, therefore, there is a question of command responsibility. It is true that if we have to act as if there were boxes into boxes into boxes and go into every single element which comes from another country, which comes from any source of investigation, in order to get to the problem where we say that in the end the Prosecutor under the supervision of the Defence must look himself for exculpatory material, and if the Defence were then able to look through all the drawers of all three floors of this building, searching for exculpatory material, I am not saying that this would be objectively speaking wrong, but I do believe that we would get into unreasonable time periods in order to deal with these proceedings. The Trial Chamber feels that for the time being this question should be put aside. If, during the course of the trial, some of the elements which arise come from another trial, the Judges will, therefore, have the responsibility to ask that discovery be made for that. Of course, closed hearings allow the Judges and would allow the Judges at that point in an ex parte proceeding, allow the three Judges, in order to see what documents come from another case. Therefore, the Trial Chamber is eliminating this issue which has to do with the Rajic case. I think I can speak for my colleagues when I say that we will work the same way for the request J. I ask my colleagues whether we should agree that. We have dealt with K. Now there is only L having to do with the databases. I give you the floor once again, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The concern here, your Honours, is that the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor possesses one or more very large and very extensive databases that have been compiled literally over a period of years. They contain more information, by definition, than what any individual can personally be familiar with. They are an electronic database and there is a reason for that, because the data is so voluminous it is more than what any person or even group of people can maintain familiarity with. That creates a special danger in a case where one party has, the Prosecution has, possession of this vast store of material; that is that that vast store of material will be used together with a filter to filter out from that huge body of material anything and everything that the Prosecution can find that is inculpatory, and then they use it to the detriment or attempt to use it to the detriment of the accused. If the Defence does not have access to the database, even indirectly, it raises the question, "Will no one search the database for exculpatory material?" Will it simply be unreviewed, unfiltered, in other words, no material will be pulled out through an exculpatory filter so that this Tribunal gets a balanced picture of the relevant evidence from that vast database? That is our concern. We are not trying to get into their confidential files and review them and take information to which we are not entitled, but I can tell this Trial Chamber that when I first asked for exculpatory material in August, I was told by letter response: "If you only would let us interview your client, we might know what you were after and we could give you a specific response". That was the response of the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor to my request in August. So, what we have done in this motion is spell out in the earlier section what we think is exculpatory. Here, with respect to databases, we think the database has significant material in it and we think it should be reviewed. We think the fairest way to ensure that there is not an imbalance in the information presented to the Tribunal would be for the parties or the Trial Chamber to select an independent Ombudsman, someone not connected with the Defence, to take, for example, the request for exculpatory information contained in our motion and have access, proper access, to the Prosecution's database, to look for any actual exculpatory material. If they found any, they could present it to the Prosecution and propose its disclosure. If the Prosecution disagreed, that Ombudsman could submit it to the Trial Chamber for a decision. We, the Defence, would have no direct access, get no information from the database without either the consent and approval of the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber. That is our proposal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like to turn to the Office of the Prosecutor. Is there a database? Could the Defence have access to it? Third, having to do with the proposal of appointing some kind of an Ombudsman or amicus curiae, perhaps amicus curiae, who would be an expert, and which would be mean that the Defence would not have direct access to the database. Could you tell us again what your opinion about this is, what the points of dispute or agreement are?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The first area of dispute is the suggestion that the Prosecutor will not review information in the databases and will filter out through the process of review only inculpatory material and not present to the Defence exculpatory material. That is an area of dispute which we hotly reject. We recognise our obligations under Rule 68. We have complied with those obligations from the beginning of this case. So that is one area of dispute. A second area of dispute ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Hold on a second. I am not sure the interpretation was right. Could you please repeat once again what are the points of dispute and what the points of agreement are? You said that you had a point of dispute. Could you please give me a more precise definition of what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The point of dispute that we have is the suggestion by the Defence that the Prosecutor will ignore her responsibilities under Rule 68 in respect of databases; we will not. The second area of dispute is a legal point, and that is whether Article 21 of the Statute of the Tribunal requires, essentially, the access to our databases. I have put forth in my response a legal point of view that Article 21 has nothing to do with discovery. It has to do with other procedural rights in the trial. I want to also essentially clarify a point that was raised, and that is a letter that has been mentioned by the Defence in this case. That letter, apparently, was written in August. It is a letter that also has other communication in it and previous communication, that says, "We have and continue to provide you with exculpatory material". The statement that has been taken and referred to by counsel is not and should not be interpreted by this Trial Chamber as a condition precedent, that is, the interview of General Blaskic, the continuing interview of General Blaskic, to our fulfilling our obligations under Rule 68. It was not. That characterization, we would submit to this Court, as the intention of the Prosecutor has not been the intention of the Prosecutor. Our response in respect of permitting a third party to have access to highly sensitive documents that are in the possession of the Prosecutor is something that we oppose for the reason that we will fulfil our obligations under Rule 68, and it is a proposal that, in reality, would permit the Defence or a third party to examine sensitive and very highly sensitive information relating to other investigations that we have in our possession. We believe that we are fully capable of abiding by our obligations in respect of the databases. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I believe that the Trial Chamber has made a list of all the problems. In my opinion and conditional on the opinion of my colleagues and of yourselves, gentlemen, I make a distinction between four main problems. The first has to do with the issue of statements. I would group them into two parts: those statements of the Prosecution and those of the witnesses. We have to know what we mean by the expression information which has been gathered or statements which have been taken. The second question -- I am going chronologically but this does not mean that this is the importance of the issues -- has to do with the Prosecution witnesses beyond factual issues. It seems that the legal issue having to do with the interpretation of 67(A) has to do with the timing when the list has to be produced. The third issue deals with all of the exculpatory materials. The issue is subdivided and in it I would put, conditional on your opinion, the proof which has been supplied by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Problem No. 3, therefore, having to do with exculpatory material would be subdivided into subparts, and I would see the demonstration that the Prosecution really does have this element, who has to determine whether this is exculpatory or inculpatory, and in the hypothesis that they must be produced, this is yet a legal important subquestion, whether or not this is a reciprocal obligation, meaning that the Defence must also supply all of its information which it is going to use in support of its client. The fourth point has to do with the databases. I am not going to connect them with the previous question, even though there is an aspect which has to do with the previous one, but I will leave it by itself because it brings out and suggests that there is an argument, not only having to do with the opinion of a third party expert or an Ombudsman who would come in and who would clarify any kinds of points in dispute, with the Defence understanding that they cannot have access to all of the databases which belong to the Prosecutor, at least not directly, but the legal question also involves the question of knowing what are the rights and the limits which can be put on those of the accused. These are the four major points. The database, the exculpatory material, the statements of the accused or of witnesses and the list of witnesses of the Prosecution, whether they should be classified in a different way. Does the Defence, first of all, agree with the list of questions as I have stated them, trying to do away with everything which is superfluous? I give you the floor, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We likewise agree, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I turn to my colleagues. Yes, we are in agreement. We will continue until 1 o'clock and, if you permit, I will give Mr. Hayman the floor who will now argue solely on those four problems, both from a legal point of view, as from a factual point of view, and we will try to get into the heart of the question. Mr. Hayman, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
