utterances.text: Turning first, your Honours, to the issue of statements, particularly statements of the accused, the first disagreement is over the interpretation of Rule 66(A), namely, whether a statement for purposes of that Rule of the accused must be produced by the Office of the Prosecution, if but only if it is a statement that was directly obtained by the Prosecutor, i.e. taken by the Prosecutor from the accused. If literally accepted, and this is the argument made in the Prosecution brief, that would mean that only statements physically taken by the Prosecutor would be within the scope of this Rule, and that would be a statement either taken as a result of the questioning or interrogation and interrogation by the Prosecutor, or a tape recording obtained by the act or acts of the Prosecutor. That also, I think, would be a statement obtained by the Prosecutor. We believe that that reading of the Rule is overly restrictive on several grounds. (1) We do not think the plain language of the Rule requires that interpretation. The phrase "all prior statements obtained by the Prosecutor from the accused" can fairly be read to mean, we think, "prior statements from or of an accused that are obtained by the Prosecutor from any source". That is how we urge the Trial Chamber to interpret the language of Rule 66(A) on this question. If that interpretation is rejected, the consequences are, for example, that a tape recording, say, of our client made by UNPROFOR, made by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and provided to the Prosecution would not be discoverable under Rule 66(A), despite I think certainly the common view in many systems, legal systems of the world, including my own, that that would be fundamentally unfair. We quote on page 3 of our reply brief the District of Columbia Circuit Court, a Federal Court, in the United States referring to "the fundamental fairness of granting the accused access to his own words, no matter how the government came by them". So the first ground of our position is the plain language of Rule 66(A) does not require their interpretation. Ours is the superior interpretation, we think. Secondly, they have suggested in their papers that there is precedent in the form of decisions of this Tribunal supporting the interpretation that a statement must be taken, directly taken, by the Prosecutor in order to constitute a statement under Rule 66(A). They cite on page 6 of their opposition brief an unofficial transcript of the Tadic matter. Through the courtesy of the Prosecution Office, I obtained a copy of this transcript yesterday. I have had a chance to look at it. I submit that it is neither precedent nor is it persuasive. It is not, in fact, a decision of any sort. What happened, apparently, in this situation was there had been an agreement between counsel as to the handling of certain letters. This is the transcript, for the record, what I was provided, it is an unofficial transcript, beginning 23rd October 1996 at 5663 and continuing through 5670 of that date, and then one page from the following day, Thursday 24th October 1996 at page 5673. What this transcript reveals is that there was an agreement between counsel to deal with these letters and that if the Prosecution was going to use them they would produce them to the Defence. A discussion came up, it appears, at the end of a trial day concerning whether one letter that had not been provided to the Defence might be discoverable under Rule 66(A) as a statement of the accused. The Presiding Judge states in part: "I certainly do not want to rule on more than what is before us, and that was not my intention to open a whole discussion of letters. It was to deal with this one Exhibit. I intend it to be that way, that is, let us see if we can work just this one problem out and not deal with the whole issue." That is on page 5669. The next morning, it appears, the Court commented: "The Trial Chamber has considered the issue and considers", referring to letters of Mr. Tadic, "that they do not constitute statements". The Trial Chamber did make that statement. By the way, there had been no argument on the issue, there had been no citation of any authority. The parties immediately informed the Court: "We reached an agreement on this. I am going to give him the letter so there is no problem". So there was no further discussion. Similarly, there is no articulation of why the Presiding Judge of Trial Chamber II made the statement that I believe she did not consider the letters to constitute statements. So I do not think, with all due respect to the judicial officer that made that statement in that transcript, that is either precedent, nor is it some persuasive authority because, in fact, it is not a decision. There is no explanation of the reasoning, much less any discussion of any authority, nor any presentation of competing authorities by the two parties to that case in connection with that decision. What we do know is that in the Delalic matter the Court in that case did make the statement that Rule 66(A) requires the Prosecution, "to disclose all statements of the accused that it has in its possession". That is at page 5 of the opinion that has been referred to in the papers as the Delalic decision of 26th September 1996. So to the extent there have been any decisions of this Tribunal on this issue, we think they favour our position. In all candour, however, I want to tell the Court that no other court, no other Trial Chamber, no other decision that we found, discusses this particular issue in a focused way. It appears there has not been a full presentation and argument on this issue of what is a statement under 66(A) for purposes of the Prosecution's discovery obligation. So, I do not think there are meaningful authorities in any direction on this coming from prior decisions of this Tribunal. Thirdly, our third ground for arguing that our interpretation should be followed here is that to find that statements need not have been taken directly by the Prosecution would be in accord with customary international law, namely, the decisions and procedures of other national legal systems. Again we have not undertaken a comprehensive review, but I can state the systems I am familiar with, certainly my own, such statements would be required to be produced and not pursuant to any reciprocal discovery scheme, but an absolute obligation on the part of the Prosecution to produce to the accused the accused's own statements in a criminal case against that individual. That is the first area of disagreement under statements. The second area of disagreement is whether a statement must be a formal statement and there, as I referred to earlier, on page 6 of the Prosecution opposition brief, they make the assertion that a statement "is a formal declaration given under oath or at least signed or acknowledged by the defendant as a true and accurate rendition." By the way, there is no citation of any authority, either within this Tribunal or in Black's Law Dictionary or anywhere else in connection with that proposition that they put forward. First, we do not agree, of course. First, I would like to point out that Rule 66(A) has no such limitation. Rule 66(A) refers to "all prior statements". It does not say, "All prior formal statements". It does not say, "All sworn statements", it does not say, "All adopted statements." It says, "All prior statements", and the Prosecution should not be allowed to impose their own greatly constricting interpretation of that phrase. Secondly, we suggest that the interpretation offered by the Prosecution lacks a reasonable basis and should be rejected on that ground as well. To accept their position would require that notes of a defendant, his own handwritten notes, would not be subject to discovery under 66(A) because they are neither sworn nor signed nor acknowledged with any formalities. We disagree with that. We think that is counter, and we think that is not reasonable. Then, lastly, we submit that their restrictive interpretation of statement does not have a basis in customary international law, and we do cite in our reply brief footnote 5 at page 4 a pertinent authority of a national court stating that with respect to Rule 16 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure in the United States that that rule "cannot be read" -- excuse me: "It is certain that 'statements'" in paragraph A1A of that Rule cannot be read to mean 'formal' statements by defendants". So at least that system has expressly rejected the formal statement limitation with respect to the term "statements" in connection with the type of discovery we are talking about, discovery of an accused's statements.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, have you concluded what you had to say about the problems of the statements of the accused which I think you are referring to as well when you speak about the declarations and statements of the witness? Have you finished with this first issue which is in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I may add, we think those arguments apply with equal force to witnesses, statements of witnesses, not just statements of the accused, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In agreement with my colleagues, we will give the Prosecutor the floor immediately so that he can answer and then the first problem which has been identified will be settled, at least provisionally, for these discussions which we are holding today. I now give you the floor, Prosecution, to respond to the first problem which has been identified having to do with the statements of the accused and witnesses, and the two subproblems, our interpretation of sub-rule 66(A) having to do with what the word "statement" means and what the word "official" is. Mr. Harmon, are you the one who will be answering?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am, your Honour, that is correct. Your Honour, first and foremost, the Prosecutor is anxious to receive guidance from the Trial Chamber on this important issue. The Prosecutor has no desire whatsoever to obstruct discovery in any way, shape or form. We are anxious to comply with it. We have continued to comply with it in good faith. In respect of Rule 66, which contains the phrase "our obligation to provide to the Defence all prior statements obtained by the Prosecutor from the accused", our reading of that, the plain language of that, particular provision is precisely what it says, that is, that the statement to be discoverable under Rule 66(A), not other provisions but under Rule 66(A) is limited. It is limited to those statements that are obtained by us from the accused. That is not to say that the accused's statements, his other statements, that are outside those obtained by us from him are not discoverable. They clearly are. They are discoverable if they are made part of the supporting material under Rule 66(A). They are discoverable if they are intended to be used as evidence under Rule 66(B) after the accused has made a request to examine them. They are discoverable as evidence at trial that were obtained under Rule 66(B) as well, because it would be, and I quote, "as evidence at trial or obtained from the accused". They are also discoverable, your Honour, as potentially exculpatory evidence as well. My reading of Rule 66(A) is that Rule 66(A) is designed to ensure that Article 21(iv)(A) has been complied with. Article 21(iv)(A) states that the defendant must be informed properly of the nature and the cause of the charges against him. So, in the context of Rule 66(A), which is disclosure of material, supporting materials, and statements from witnesses and from the accused, our view, we would submit, your Honour, and a reasonable view, is that that Rule is designed to inform him properly of the cause and the nature of the charges against him. I think it is very important for this Trial Chamber to consider the Rules of Evidence and Procedure as a whole, because I think, if viewed in isolation, each of these Rules has the capacity to render null any of the other Rules that are contained in the structure, the scheme that has been set up by the Judges, to ensure the trial is fair and to ensure that you, your Honours, receive information and evidence that will assist you in making a fair determination of the facts. When I say, for example, that each of these Rules has the capacity to consume any of the other Rules, let me point out, for example, that when the Defence requests as statements on page 7 of his motion, item No. 2, all written letters, notes, ledgers, orders or other writings either written by the accused or containing statements known or believed by the Prosecution to be statements of the accused, and in referring to page 8, item No. 1, where he asks for all written statements, including declarations, transcripts, memoranda of interviews, situation reports, intelligence reports, teletypes and other forms of military messages and substantially verbatim interview notes of the investigators, if the word "statement", the term "statement", is giving that broad meaning, it will, in essence, make Rule 66(B) irrelevant, because the defendant by characterising all of those documents, all of those statements, which he clearly has access to, should he make a request under 66(B), it will make Rule 66(B) moot. Therefore, it is our position, your Honour, that the term "statements" in the context of Rule 66(A) has limits. Those limits were set forth and articulated clearly by the Judges who promulgated these Rules. They could have used the word "of"; they chose instead to use the words "all prior statements obtained by the Prosecutor from the accused". So, our view, your Honours, is that Rule 66(A) has been complied with by the Prosecutor and there is a limitation by Rule 66(A). Obviously, in our efforts to look for some form of precedent, we have relied upon or in part presented in our brief the Tadic decision, a decision relating to a single item, a letter, which is similar to that requested by the accused in this case. Our submission to the Court is it is for whatever weight this Court deems appropriate; if the Court feels that decision is helpful in forming its judgment, then we have submitted it for that purpose and no other purpose. In respect of the Rules of this Court, however, I would turn to Rule 89(A) which says that the Chambers are not bound by Rules of evidence from various nations. This is an opportunity by this International Tribunal to develop its own unique set of Rules that it deems appropriate, that it thinks should govern the conduct of trials. I would submit to this Court that the reciprocal discovery provisions of the Rules which this Court thought were an appropriate set of Rules governing the trials and the information process that comes to your Honours, that is a set of provisions that are not found necessarily in all national systems, but that is not the test. The test, your Honours, is certainly your Honours may create Rules that can govern the submission and the development of evidence as it deems appropriate. Reciprocal discovery provisions are clearly in the Rules. They are intended to provide an opportunity to the Defence to have access to all of the documents which he now seeks to obtain, or most of the documents he seeks to obtain, by claiming that they are statements. We think that that position is untenable. We think it would subvert the Rules and we submit that there has to be and should be a limitation on what constitutes statements in the context of Rule 66(A). I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Deschenes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, Mr. Hayman has referred us to the decision rendered by another Chamber of this Tribunal in the matter of Delalic last September. You are, no doubt, familiar with that decision. I am somewhat puzzled by a couple of lines which I just would like to bring back into the debate. At page 5 the Chamber was discussing exactly, I think, the problem that we have now. At page 5, at about line 9 or 10 the Chamber writes as follows: "The second type of material is 'all prior statements obtained by the Prosecutor from the accused'". Unless I am mistaken -- I am stopping here, Mr. Harmon -- this is precisely the phrase which you have been debating a moment ago as well as Mr. Hayman. I am continuing then with the Delalic decision which then says: "This part of the Rule requires the Prosecution to disclose all statements of the accused that it has in its possession." I am just asking the question. I am puzzled, as I say, does not that part of the decision go a long way in support of the position taken by Mr. Hayman or of the interpretation that he has been trying to give to the Rule, or what interpretation would you yourself put on that decision in Delalic, in the light of your dispute now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that underscores the reason we have a dispute in this case. The decision seems to be somewhat contradictory in this respect. We, obviously, are before your Honours seeking guidance of this Chamber in our dispute to resolve this dispute. I have submitted to this Chamber what the Prosecutor views as a reasonable interpretation of the plain language of Rule 66(A).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: But could you not consider this decision in Delalic as the guidance which the Prosecution needs? Apparently, you are not satisfied with that decision and you want us to decide somewhat differently. Am I wrong in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I refer then the Court in the same opinion to a few lines further down? In paragraph 4, the last sentence, "In summary, Rule 66(A) requires the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence all supporting materials that accompany the indictment at the confirmation, all prior statements obtained by the Prosecution from the accused", and it goes on. So there are different parts of the opinion that give rise to our dispute. My view is, yes, if you take that sentence, that is, in isolation, that requires the Prosecution to disclose all statements of the accused that it has in its possession, it clearly supports Mr. Hayman's position.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just a one minute rebuttal, perhaps, your Honour? That is, I think that ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. No. Go ahead, but just a moment. Do not speak too long, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand. I think Mr. Harmon's argument that the structure of the Rules compel a conclusion that statements in 66(A) only include statements obtained directly from the Prosecutor by the accused would have weight if 66(B) referred to other statements or statements of the accused or witnesses obtained from other parties or something like that. But there is not a word, not a letter, in 66(B) suggesting that in any way it is contemplated that there are other statements that, of course, a defendant is going to get under 66(B) if the accused triggers the reciprocal discovery Rules. On the contrary, 66(B) speaks of books, documents, photographs and tangible objects which, I think, is a different category.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we will stop the discussion on this point. We could get into all kinds of semantics and interpretations. This has even been appealed. You are looking at us as if we were the Appeals Chamber, but in any case the Trial Chamber will respond in the light of the debate that it has heard and looking at the various decisions which have been taken in one direction or another. It is now 12.30. As I said, we will go on until 1 o'clock, since there are a few other questions to be dealt with. We will give the floor back to Mr. Hayman so that we can deal with of the three other legal questions in the order which he would like. It does not matter which order he chooses. We give you the floor, Mr. Hayman, and then we will give the floor to the Prosecutor for his response.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I think witness list is a short item and I would go to it next. Our position is that under Rule 67(A) as early as reasonably practicable, which is the language of that Rule, requires the provision of a witness list when the Prosecution first forms an intent to call certain witnesses and not to call others at trial. If they have no such intent, they cannot identify one witness that they currently intend to call at trial, then I think they have an obligation to tell us that at this hearing. But if they have an intent to call any witness or any group of witnesses, a present intention to do so, they should give us a list of such witnesses and they have, of course, an obligation to update that list; I am not saying on a daily basis, but on a reasonable basis they have an obligation to update that list. So if there are, for example, a significant number of witnesses whose identities have been disclosed to us but whom they do not intend to call, we are able to prioritize and intelligently prepare for trial in the time remaining. That is the purpose of this Rule, so that we have a list of the names of witnesses that they intend to call. We still do not have that. We think we should have that and we would suggest that, unless they can say they have no intention, no current intent to call anyone, that a date certain be set, perhaps in seven days time, to give us a list.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. This question must form the basis for an agreement, even if it is an agreement to disagree. Prosecutor, you have obligations pursuant to 67(A). In the previous debate which fuelled our work, you know that we had a trial date which was for 8th January, as I remember, and that, for various reasons, we were obliged to postpone for an indefinite time. Therefore, in any event, you would have been prepared, even if I know that you had challenged the date of 8th January, to provide that list. It is true that the accused does have to know what is the current list of all of the witnesses that the Prosecution has. What do you think about this, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have a dispute as to the Rule because the Rule itself is very flexible. The Rule says that we have to turn over our witness list as soon as practicable or, in any event, prior to trial. There is no trial date in this case. There are hearings set on motions and I want to assure this Court that we fully intend also to comply with Rule 67(A). However, I want to point out to this Court something that it may already be aware of, and that is that I came on to this case in the middle of October of this year. Prior to that, I was not involved in this particular case or any case related to it. Currently, your Honour, I should say, we intend in the very near future after the Christmas holidays to sit down and start preparing a witness list. When we do that, we will give that forthwith to the Defence. Their request to have an order that we submit a witness list to them in seven days is unreasonable. It cannot be complied with by us, very frankly, but we will endeavour to give them a witness list as soon as we can. But I need time to study this case ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, excuse me to intervene, but really if I were in the position of defendant counsel I would find myself rather in an uncomfortable position. You put the Defence in the position of saying, yes, indeed you rely on us, the Prosecution, we are faithful to our duties, we know what we have do, and we will give you a list of our witnesses as soon as possible. But what does that mean in so far as the Defence is concerned? It is likely, on the basis of what we know now, that this trial will take place some time in the coming spring. As soon as possible, what is possible for you may not have the same appearance as what is possible for the Defence and the point of view is obviously quite diametrically opposed. Do you not think that even though it may be that within seven days may be a little short, on the other hand, when possible, may be a little long. It would not be unreasonable that some reasonable delay be fixed now so that the Defence knows within the foreseeable future if and when it will ever receive a list of witnesses and what it will do with it. It seems to me to be realistic that we should be in a position to pinpoint a certain date. After all, you have already given, I do not know, 100 statements or thereabouts. So you have least a constructive list that exists at least. I know nothing of your file nor of your work and so on, but I suggest that after saying seven days is not enough, it is not enough either on the other side just to say, "When we can and "When it is possible".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have informed this Court what I intend to do. I intend after the Christmas holidays to sit down with staff and start formulating that witness list. That will occur roughly in the middle of January, those discussions. I will then be quite willing to provide to the Defence a list of witnesses who we have the present intention of calling. Clearly I think a witness list, your Honour, is something that has to be flexible. It cannot be something that is etched in stone because this trial process, as this Court is aware is dynamic process. We have had, for example, witnesses who have said early on in the investigation that they were prepared to be witnesses, they are no longer prepared to be witnesses. So it is an evolving process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Nobody will question that and I think we are getting closer to a realistic answer to the question that is raised by the Defence. I have heard mid-January as the time when you plan to sit down and work on this thing, conceivably to come to an end not long after that. So, already we have something that is far better coming from the Prosecution than the only "if possible". Could I suggest that maybe going alone that line you might say, well, a first tentative list at least will be transmitted to the Defence by such a date as you would suggest and we would have the burden here to find whether it is acceptable or not, but please do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, assuming our discussions, and I am quite confident they will proceed on schedule in the middle of January and they will be extensive discussions, we are prepared to give a preliminary list of witnesses to the Defence at the beginning of February, February 1st. I recall, your Honour, I am not certain on this point, there may have been a similar discussion and debate in the Tadic case. I have heard this, but I cannot say this for sure. My recollection is that there was an order of the Trial Chamber to provide a witness list I think 30 days before the commencement of trial. So, we are quite happy to meet with ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is a problem we are going to settle right now. This Trial Chamber has deliberated over this issue. You must supply us with this list by 1st February at the latest. It is self-evident that the list may change and that between the date 1st February and the date that the trial will begin, there may be other witnesses whose names should be included. Three Judges have taken into account the problem, not that you have gone about this with a great deal of delays, that is not what he have taken into account. What we have taken into account is the difficulties of this case, the presentation of the arguments on both sides and your own contingencies having to do with your staff. So 1st February will be the list of witnesses as complete and as up-to-date as possible, a complete list of witnesses, between 1s February and the date which the trial begins. This may be changed only in relation to the elements of the investigation which may have taken place in the meantime. Does this satisfy you? This is your own proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are quite happy to provide the witness list as we believe it to exist on February 1st, obviously taking into consideration changing events that may impact on that list. If we continue, as we do intend to do, this investigation and develop other witnesses whom we intend to call, we will present the names of those witnesses as well to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The second issue deserves to be settled by the Judges here at the Bench. We give you the floor again now, Mr. Hayman, in order to take up one of the two remaining questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think your Honour the remaining category is exculpatory information, although it has some subcategories to it. The gist of the disagreement as we see it is that we did make an enquiry in August for exculpatory information, and we were told that the Prosecution could respond more specifically but only if they had more information from us, and they specifically asked for a further interviews with our client which we have declined. Instead we have provided them with approximately eight pages of specific information that we believe that they have or nowhere it exists. Under Rule 68 they have an obligation to produce exculpatory information that they possess and inform us of any such evidence the existence of which is known to the Prosecution. So what we seek is a statement from them on the record whether they have or know of the existence of the material we seek. If they do not, they should say so. If they do have it or know of it, then they either need to tell us that they are going to give it to us or that they think it is not exculpatory which then creates a specific issue as to a specific category of information that can be addressed perhaps with the assistance of the Trial Chamber. But the current response of the Prosecutor, namely that they will not say whether they have it or not and they also contest whether it is exculpatory, leaves us with no basis to resolve, one, to identify what the dispute really is or, two, to resolve it. We need to be able to resolve it because we feel very strongly that this information is information that we must have and should have in order to obtain a fair trial for our client. The last of the three issues that the Prosecutor identified, that of reciprocity, I do not understand what that has to do with this issue. Rule 68 has no reciprocal discovery obligation. It is a unilateral obligation on the part of the Prosecution, and I simply do not understand the argument he is making there so I cannot state what our response is to it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If I were to summarise, I can give the floor to the Prosecutor, does he recognise that he has all of these elements? What kind of statement would the Prosecutor make about this, and then the question of reciprocal disclosure of the evidence? Mr. Harmon, would you care to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you, I would like to say something. First of all, as I said earlier in my remarks, we do recognise our obligation under Rule 68 and it is not a fair characterization in the reply of the Defence motion that we do not have an obligation to search for those materials. We do. We have embarked on that search and we continue to embark on that search. What we do have here is an eight-page list which is essentially designed to obtain access, essentially an open file access, to all of our materials that we have in our possession under the guise of it being exculpatory. This Tribunal has set up rules that deal with reciprocal discovery, and those rules should not be circumvented by claiming, without foundation, that, one, we have documents in our possession that we are not giving and, two, without a showing by the applicant, the Defence in this case, that what he is seeking to obtain is in fact exculpatory. The net result of a broad application like this is without a showing that it is exculpatory and an order by this Chamber that we have to search our materials for everything, it has the potential capacity of paralyzing the Prosecutor's Office in doing knowing but searching for things they may or may not be exculpatory. We are very happy if he points to specific items, not broad, general items like he has in his application, to attempt to locate those. Let me give you an example. If you turn, your Honours, to item 14 of his request, in item 14, your Honour, let me find the page number of that ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could you indicate what page this is, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it is page 21.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. This is the example you are going to use in order to state that this is such a broad request that it is paralyzing your office, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I wanted to say about request 14, your Honour, and it reads as follows, "Documents or information indicating that the accused was not physically present at or in the vicinity of any of the events alleged to constitute crimes in the first indictment or in the amended indictment." This is a command responsibility case, your Honour, and his criminal responsibility is both for his acts and for his omissions. He was not present at a significant number of these events that are alleged in the indictment. But what this request says is, give us all of your documents to show he was not there. In other words, give us everything that you have in your files access to because we claim this is exculpatory. So our position is, your Honour, that a defendant has to show, first of all, more than mere speculation that we have a document in our possession. He has said he has that information. He told this Chamber on page 5 of his indictment that he knew he had this information or that he had reason to believe that we had, each of these items that are listed in his eight-page request. The second point is he has to show that the items that he has requested are, arguably, exculpatory under Rule 68 and he has not demonstrated that. To permit this kind of broad-side request for discovery under the guise that this is exculpatory, as I say, has practical problems. It could paralyse us in searching virtually all the time for items he my not really truly think that we have in our possession. So, that is the practical problem. The other problem is this, your Honour. This suggests that the Prosecutor is not proceeding in good faith on its obligation to locate items that we consider are exculpatory. It is interesting to note that in his motion he has not claimed that he has not received evidence that is potentially exculpatory. He has. He has received it from the beginning of this case. He has received it in a timely fashion. In my response to his motion I point out very specifically items that were turned around very quickly. There was a potentially exculpatory piece of that was obtained by an investigator in Sarajevo on 13th December. I informed counsel of its existence. It was brought up from Sarajevo. It was translated and turned over to the Defence within two weeks. There is another example, I think it is shortly thereafter, an item that was returned to our office was potentially exculpatory and turned over to the Defence within a very, very short period of people. So that I think, your Honour, is important in your consideration as to whether or not we are proceeding in good faith to meet our obligations under Rule 68. That is our position in this regard. We will continue to seek information and search for information that is potentially exculpatory and provide it to him on a timely basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a very broad and complex question. I will give you the floor, Mr. Hayman, in a second. I would like to make another comment. This question is not dealt in the same way in the various legal systems. The one I know the best does not produce these kinds of questions, because we have an investigating and magistrate not the Prosecutor who gathers the inculpatory and exculpatory evidence in the case file all through its progress with both parties being heard. I do not know if there could be a sort of in between period, because at the same time what the Defence uses in its arguments in support of his thesis has been presented. It is true we cannot ask the Prosecutor to be completely the Prosecutor and as well counsel for the Defence. So I ask this question for myself and I will give you the floor then, Mr. Hayman. Could there not be an agreement which has been suggested by the Prosecutor, that is the minimum of evidence which must be supplied to you, that is, instead of saying "give us the entire case file", "give us the entire case file and we will do what we need to do and we will go fishing, if you like, for everything that would be of interest to us and in support of what we have to say." Perhaps you also must set up a list, conditional on what my colleagues have to say who are perhaps more familiar with this system, but a specific list saying at this day or at this time we say that when it comes to an offence which was launched by the HVO, for example, in this or that area, that my client, as is shown in the documents which you have, was not there. This is an example. Perhaps this is a suggestion, but it might be more specific at the same time. I will turn to my colleagues to ask what their comments might be about this. (The Learned Judges conferred).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, just in the same line as what the President mentioned, you gave us a double message, that the goodwill is there to give exculpatory evidence, but practically it is impossible. Is that what I understood? Practically you would be doing the job of the Defence. What was the message exactly you gave us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have given you the message, your Honour, that we intend to search our files for potentially exculpatory evidence. What I am saying to your Honours is if it is a broad, speculative list of items that the Defence believes we have in our possession and we are obligated to go searching through all our vast materials based on his speculations, then it has the potential to paralyse us. Let me give you, your Honour, an example as well. Item No. 13 which he requests is very precise. Item No. 13 refers to part of the confirming materials in Rule 47. He identifies with specificity an item. That item has been given to the Defence already, but the ability to say something very specifically, this particular item we can comply with. A broad-side request, "give us all documents showing that he was not physically there", will take us for ever to search, to locate and, frankly, is not warranted under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I too am hearing multiple statements by the Prosecution. They assure the Defence that they will produce all exculpatory material and that they will proceed in good faith to do that, but they disagree that our list of information is exculpatory. That still does not give us any mechanism for resolving those disputes. If they do not think something in our list is exculpatory, that is, let me eliminate that double negative. If they think something is not exculpatory they need to say so, so that we can get a decision from the Trial Chamber on that. Obviously they are not going to look for anything if they think it is not exculpatory. They think they will have no obligation under that circumstance. So they are mixing a bunch of different messages together, and I think the result is a message that is less than coherent. I would like to make a proposal in that regard, but before doing that one other comment on our request No. 14. They belittle request No. 14 concerning the whereabouts of our client on the grounds that this is a command responsibility case. In the amended indictment they also charge the accused in paragraph 5.6 with planning, instigating, ordering, committing or otherwise aiding and abetting in the preparation, planning or execution of the acts. So he is charged in this amended indictment both as a direct participant and as a Commander with command responsibility for the acts. Committing, he is charged with committing the acts. That is in paragraph 5.6 of the indictment. It may well be a burden on them to identify the information they that shows that our client could not have committed a charged act because he was not there, but, by golly, they charged him in paragraph 5.6 with committing the acts in the amended indictment. If they have information that he was not there and that he could not have committed it, then they have to go through their files and their database however voluminous they are and give us that information because that is what Rule 68 requires. If they did not mean to charge him with that, then they should take that out of the indictment. How do we work our way out of this? I am perfectly willing if there is a request that we have made that is insufficiently specific, to try to make it more specific so that the Prosecution can focus their search. However, there are a number of our requests which cannot be made more specific. For example, paragraph 1, if our client directed to military personnel that they must adhere to a rule that requires the protection of civilians, we have got to have that for the trial in this case. Whether it was in July 1992 or October 1993 or whenever during the time period of the indictment, we have to have it and they have an obligation to give it to us. So there are some of these requests that cannot be made more specific. I suggest that the Trial Chamber order the Prosecutor within a reasonable period of time, whether that is seven days or 14 days or whatever, to indicate in writing to us whether, first, they contest that any information specified in our motion is in fact exculpatory. If they say it is not exculpatory, then we can respond to that and we can get a decision from the Trial Chamber, because so long as that is grey and unresolved we do not know what they are going to look for and give us even if they happen to run across it inadvertently. So there has to be some agreement, given that we have specified what we think is exculpatory, whether they agree or disagree, otherwise we will never know what they gave us out of the universe. That is inappropriate, because the accused is entitled to a decision and some direction on whether or not he in fact is entitled to such material, the material we have taken the trouble to specify. So I submit that would be the first they should be directed to do, to tell us if they disagree regarding whether something is exculpatory. Secondly, if they would tell us whether something is too broad and too general, I will agree, we will do our best to make it more specific. But if they do not contest that it is exculpatory and they do not believe that a request has to be more specific, then they have an obligation to look for any such material and give it to the Defence. I submit they have an obligation to do that even before they do their own work and prepare their own case. Nowhere in the Rules does it say they have to prepare their own case by a certain date before trial, but under Rule 68 they have got to give us exculpatory information as soon as practicable. So I submit that would be a working format for working through these issues and getting them resolved. I have not heard any meaningful proposal from the Prosecution in that regard.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I believe this is a very complex and broad problem about which the Trial Chamber will deliberate. Both the Defence and the Prosecution, we must find a point of balance. When we look at 1(i) in order to explain how we might reach a point of balance, in 1(i) you have listed the crimes which are alleged to be committed by the HVO. I do understand what this could be used for in order to support the Defence of your client, but if in fact really the Prosecutor were to go about a very thorough investigation which the HVO might have committed, that is an investigation within an investigation, we know your application has 14 points, but if we just look at point No. 1 from (A) all the way to (L) and beyond, I believe that the Trial Chamber, and this is its duty, will decide what the point of balance must be. This is the role of the Judges to interpret the Rules of Procedure and Evidence according to the system, but also within a system that is part of the Rules. The Prosecutor cannot take the place of the Defence. The Defence has rights which, as Judges responsible for having everything being respected, we must find a balance point so that the rights of General Blaskic are completely protected, but at the same time the Prosecutor must be able to go forward, otherwise the Defence could not later complain that this trial keeps being constantly delayed. That is the responsibility of the Judges which they will assume. I will put an end to the review of this third point and we will begin again at 2.30 or, if you prefer, 3 o'clock. We have still one more point to be spoken about, at least I believe. Mr. Hayman, do you feel you have taken up all the issues? There is the question of database included in your argument about point 3, in other words, point 4 where there was a dispute having to do with access to the database with the problem of confidentiality and secrets. When we look at 21, do you want to argue very quickly now or do you think you have already argued within 3, 4.4 which would mean that this hearing is now complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think with respect to databases we have stated our request, they have stated their objection and it is properly submitted. Unless the Trial Chamber has any concerns or questions about this issue of reciprocity which I still do not understand, I think we are prepared to submit the motion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Having do to do with reciprocity I do have a question. What is your proposal about reciprocity, complete reciprocity for all of these documents having to do with the exculpatory evidence which is part of the Rules? What is your position on that, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have not made a request for reciprocal discovery and we do not intend to. It is our position that the provisions for reciprocal discovery by the Defence in the Tribunal Rules violate the right of an accused to remain silent, the fact that the obligation is on the Prosecution to go forward and they have the burden, the accused has no burden of producing evidence, and based on the fact that we believe there is asymmetry in the Rules concerning the privileges and protections afforded to Prosecution evidence that are not afforded to any evidence the Defence has. So we do not intend to make a request triggering reciprocal discovery in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, do you have any comments you would like to make about reciprocity, the reciprocal discovery, because this is an issue which has come up at various points?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, thank you. We clearly believe that the reciprocity provisions are fair, and that they are consistent with both Article 21 and Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The Rules of reciprocal discovery are Rules that this Tribunal decided were necessary and fair and should be used if the defendant so requested, in order to assist in the truth-seeking process. These Rules have been invoked by other defendants. They are workable and manageable. It is clearly the defendant's right to not invoke aspects of the Rules of procedure that are contained therein. However, our view is that while he rejects the reciprocal discovery provisions of the Rules, and we have addressed our views on that in our response to his motion requesting that they be declared void, he should not be permitted to obtain through the clever use and request under other rules to receive precisely what he could receive had he made a request under reciprocal discovery. So our position is that those Rules are valid. The motion to compel discovery is tantamount to a one-sided request to see all the Prosecutor's file and not permit to the Prosecutor to see the evidence he intends to produce at trial. That is our view on the matter, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, one last point before we close the discussions. What difference do you make in this long list of documents about which you were asking? What I am asking, legally speaking and statutorily speaking, what difference do you make between the rights which you are invoking under Rule 68 and the rights of 66(B) which allows you to look at any photographs or other documents which the Prosecution may have which would be required for the Defence of the accused? What connection do you make? For the time being I know what you have done or that you have not done at least, so we are not asking and we will not make any application pursuant to 66(B) which, of course, shelters you from reciprocal discovery which is provided for under 66(B). However, I remain persuaded that there is a question which has not been made raised. Nonetheless, in 68 the Prosecutor must communicate a large group of documents, and in the long list you are asking for documents and all kinds of Prosecution evidence. What is it that you are asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are asking under the exculpatory evidence portion of our motion for information, information that may tend to assist us in the defence of our client. We believe the Prosecution has under Rule 68 an absolute obligation to give that to us. Whatever the threshold is, and the materiality in Rule 68 uses the standard "which in any way tends to suggest or mitigate the guilt of the accused". That is what we are asking for. We have detailed the information because we were not getting any exculpatory information from the Prosecution, but we have started to get a couple of documents since we filed our motion. So that is why we detailed it. We do not see a link, and there is no link I submit, between our motion and our list of requested information. Rule 66(B) is a different procedure that other defendants may choose to utilize. We make no such choice and we are not going to utilize the discovery provisions of Rule 68(B).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Unless the Prosecutor wishes to supplement something or has any other comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional comments, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have now dealt with all the disputes which remained having to do with discovery. The hearing is adjourned and the Trial Chamber will render its decision in January at a date which will be made public later by the Registrar. The Court stands adjourned. My colleagues and I wish everybody a merry Christmas and a happy New Year. 1.10 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: (The hearing adjourned for a short time)
